brief.desc: BEARISH, 40/100. Friday was a relief bounce inside a downtrend still set by a 2.9% real yield and a Fed that hiked in September. The sell-off has stalled, not reversed, and confidence is moderate pending Wednesday's CPI.
brief.yr: GLD closed $384.58 (+1.57%) and gold futures settled $4,216.30 (+1.43%) on Friday October 9, with spot at $4,194.46 (+1.44%). The move was not explained by Friday's closes: Treasury's 10y real yield rose 4bp to 2.91% and DXY was flat at 102.21. The impulse came from strong 10y and 30y auctions that pulled yields off highs on October 8, Trump's pledge of no Iran strike before the midterms, and fading October hike odds. Futures peaked at $4,233.70, short of the $4,251.10 September 30 high, in a narrow gap-and-hold session.
brief.to: Base case (50%) is a $4,100 to $4,250 futures range drifting lower as real yields hold 2.8 to 3.0%; a hot CPI on October 14 could push futures toward $4,000 (30%), while a soft CPI and a dovish Warsh on October 16 could carry them to about $4,400 (20%). The week's events are Waller and Collins on Tuesday, CPI on Wednesday, PPI and retail sales on Thursday, and Fed Chair Warsh on Friday, with the US cash bond market closed Monday for Columbus Day. This view flips bullish if the 10-year TIPS real yield closes below 2.60%.
kf: Real yields (10y TIPS at 2.91%, +31bp in 20 days)
COMEX positioning (managed money still net long 110,987, being cut)

brief.why: The Fed's September hike reset the regime. A 12-0 vote at 3.75-4.00% told the market the committee would tighten into an energy-driven headline print (August CPI 3.4% y/y headline against 2.4% core) rather than look through it. Bonds repriced the policy path and the term premium: the 10y nominal went from 4.96% to 5.24% in 20 sessions while breakevens slipped from 2.36% to 2.33%. Investors are demanding real compensation, not inflation protection. A 2.9% real yield is a steep carry cost for a zero-coupon asset, and the dollar, up 3.1% in 20 days, compounded it for non-US buyers. COMEX speculators did the selling: WGC estimates September managed-money net fell 84t and spreads 156t, and CFTC data to October 6 show longs still being cut and shorts added. The price-insensitive bid did the buying: global ETFs took $10bn (67t) in September to a record 4,256t, and central banks added 39t in August led by the PBoC. That is why the decline paused near GLD $375-$385. In October the marginal Fed changed: October hike odds fell from about 55% to about 16-22% after the September jobs data and minutes, and auctions cleared well. That removed the next leg of the real-yield shock, which is enough for a bounce but not a reversal. Real yields are still 48bp above early September, and gold needs them to fall, not just stop rising.
brief.cons: The loud narrative is a relief rally testing the $4,251 wall, and prediction markets lean bullish, with Polymarket at 68% that gold touches $4,300 in October. The consensus that the Fed is done is mostly right on October, but it is being stretched into a claim that real yields have peaked, which the data do not yet show: the Treasury 10y real yield printed 2.91% on the day gold rallied 1.6%. The short is not crowded. Managed money was still net long 110,987 contracts with longs outnumbering shorts 7.9 to 1 on October 6, and ETF holdings are at a record. The crowded side remains long, which fits a bearish call because there is more length left to liquidate than shorts to squeeze. The risk is that record ETF holdings are sticky strategic money that will not sell, which caps the downside even if speculators keep exiting.
fals: Soften: Gold futures settle above $4,251 (the September 30 high) by Friday October 16; the bounce becomes more than relief and the call moves to neutral near 50.
Invert: The 10-year TIPS real yield closes below 2.60% (the September 11 level), most likely after the October 14 CPI; that unwinds the September shock and flips the call bullish.

Weak joint: I assume Friday's 1.6% rally was positioning noise, not gold decoupling from real yields, but CFTC data stop at October 6 and I have no October ETF flow data; if the COT due around October 16 shows managed-money longs rising or WGC shows heavy October inflows, the bearish call is wrong.
